title: A General-Purpose Molecular Foundation Model Transfers Across Olfactory Tasks
hook: Fine-tune a general molecular foundation model on one smell task and it transfers to four others untrained — including telling mirror-image molecules apart, which 2D graphs cannot.
key_points: Uni-Mol2, a general molecular foundation model, was fine-tuned on the GS-LF multi-label odor descriptor benchmark.
The resulting model was evaluated on four downstream settings with no additional deep-learning training.
Downstream tasks: cross-dataset odor descriptor prediction, odorous vs odorless classification, enantiomer evaluation, odor mixture discriminability.
It matches or exceeds the state-of-the-art olfaction-specific baseline on the primary GS-LF benchmark.
3D molecular representations distinguish enantiomers (mirror-image molecules) in a way 2D graph models cannot.
Predicting the perceptual consequences of stereochemistry remains open — distinguishing the molecules isn't the same as predicting the smell.
content_html: Foundation models reshaped molecular property prediction, but machine olfaction has largely been served by olfaction-specific models. Han and colleagues ask whether a general molecular foundation model, fine-tuned on one canonical smell task, learns representations that carry across the rest of the field.
extra_html:
The test

They fine-tune Uni-Mol2 on the GS-LF benchmark for multi-label odor descriptor prediction, then evaluate the resulting model — without additional deep-learning training — on four complementary downstream settings: cross-dataset odor descriptor prediction, odorous-versus-odorless classification, enantiomer evaluation, and odor mixture discriminability. On the primary GS-LF benchmark the fine-tuned model matches or exceeds the state-of-the-art olfaction-specific baseline, and it transfers consistently across all four downstream evaluations.

The stereochemistry result

The enantiomer analysis is the most interesting piece. Enantiomers are mirror-image molecules with identical connectivity graphs — so a 2D graph model literally cannot tell them apart, however much data you give it. The three-dimensional representations here do distinguish them. But the authors are careful about what that buys: accurately predicting the perceptual consequences of stereochemistry, which is what a perfumer would actually want, remains an open challenge. Taken together the results support a train-once, transfer-across-tasks paradigm for machine olfaction, with chemically pretrained molecular representations as the substrate. arXiv, 2026.

related.title: AlphaFold: Protein Structure Prediction
related.hook: Predicting a protein's 3D shape from its sequence stumped biology for ~50 years. AlphaFold cracked it at near-experimental accuracy — and then released the structures to everyone.

related.title: When Remembering More Slows the Search Down
related.hook: Generate molecules, score them, keep the best, retrain, repeat. A convergence theory for this drug-discovery workhorse finds that training on more of the past can actually hurt.

flashcards.prompt: What does the 'train-once, transfer-across-tasks' claim mean here?
flashcards.back_html: Fine-tune a general molecular foundation model on one canonical olfactory task (GS-LF odor descriptors), then apply it to several other olfaction problems with no further deep-learning training.

flashcards.prompt: Why do 3D molecular representations matter for enantiomers?

choices.text: Mirror-image molecules have identical 2D graphs, so only a 3D representation can distinguish them
3D representations are smaller and therefore faster to fine-tune
Enantiomers always smell identical, so 3D representations confirm the null result

flashcards.explanation_html: Enantiomers share the same connectivity graph. The paper reports 3D representations separate them in a way 2D graph models fundamentally cannot — though predicting the perceptual consequence remains unsolved.

flashcards.prompt: What does the paper say is still an open challenge?
flashcards.back_html: Accurately predicting the perceptual consequences of stereochemistry. The model can tell enantiomers apart structurally; predicting how differently they smell is another matter.
